    Summary and Setup

    Training Material 6 · Preprocessing, Harmonisation, Validation, Analysis

    This module shows how statistical programming can be used as a reproducible method for processing, harmonising, integrating, validating and analysing bibliographic data. Systematically refined bibliographic records are combined with a case study in the statistical analysis of open-access bibliographic data: Fennica, the Finnish national bibliography, with more than 70,000 publications from 1809 to 1917.

    The whole module follows one research question:

    How did the shift from Swedish to Finnish in publishing happen in 19th-century Finland, and how certain can we be about it?

    The course has five parts:

    1. Introduction to bibliographic data, MARC 21 and the tools of the course.
    2. Data description of the Finnish national bibliography.
    3. Making the data ready for analysis: cleaning with the fennica R package, harmonisation, enrichment with Finto and Finna, and validation.
    4. Basic statistical analysis: research questions answered with linear regression, the chi-squared test and other basic methods.
    5. Probabilistic analysis of how certain our answers are.

    Some episodes are still in preparation and are marked as such.

    Prerequisite

    Prerequisites

    Basic knowledge of R, including running scripts, loading packages, importing data, and performing simple data-frame operations. No prior experience with bibliographic data is required.

    Please complete the Setup instructions before the workshop.

    What you will learn

    • Cleaning: profiling raw MARC records, cleaning text fields with regular expressions, reusing the fennica package
    • Harmonisation: lookup and synonym tables, combining MARC fields, authority identifiers, writing the pipeline as reusable functions
    • Enrichment: linking records to external vocabularies and collections (Finto, Finna) through identifiers and open APIs
    • Validation: rule-based checks, comparison of independent harmonisations, non-random missingness, sensitivity of results to cleaning decisions
    • Basic statistical analysis: linear regression, the chi-squared test and other basic methods, applied to research questions
    • Probabilistic analysis: expressing the uncertainty of results based on incomplete and inconsistent data

    This lesson uses R and RStudio, the packages arrow, dplyr, tidyr, stringr, stringi, ggplot2 and jsonlite, and one dataset. Please complete the steps below before the workshop. It takes about 20–30 minutes.

    Software Setup

    Discussion

    Details

    You need a recent version of R (4.1 or later) and RStudio Desktop. Both are free. If you already have them installed, make sure R is up to date: the code uses the native pipe |>, which requires R 4.1 or later. Check your version by typing R.version.string in the R console.

    1. Download and install R from CRAN.
    2. Download and install RStudio Desktop.
    1. Download and install R from CRAN. Choose the version for your processor (Apple silicon or Intel).
    2. Download and install RStudio Desktop.
    1. Install R by following the instructions for your distribution on CRAN.
    2. Download and install RStudio Desktop.

    Install the R packages

    Open RStudio and run this line in the console:

    R 

    install.packages(c("arrow", "dplyr", "tidyr", "stringr", "stringi", "ggplot2", "jsonlite"))

    Check that the installation worked by loading each package. You should not see any errors (messages about masked objects are fine):

    R 

    library(arrow)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(jsonlite)

    Data Sets

    We use a harmonised extract of Fennica, the Finnish national bibliography, covering publications from 1809 to 1917 (72,626 records, about 16 MB).

    1. In RStudio, create a new project: File > New Project > New Directory > New Project. Call it, for example, fennica-r.

    2. In the project folder, create a folder called data.

    3. Download the data file harmonized_fennica19.feather from CSC’s object storage and save it in the data folder.

      You can also download it directly from R. Run this in the RStudio console with your project open:

      R 

      dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
download.file(
  "https://a3s.fi/swift/v1/AUTH_3c0ccb602fa24298a6fe3ae224ca022f/fennica-container/output.tables/harmonized_fennica19.feather",
  destfile = "data/harmonized_fennica19.feather",
  mode = "wb"
)

      (mode = "wb" makes sure the file is saved correctly on Windows.)

    4. For the episodes on harmonisation and validation you also need the raw catalogue records, priority_fields19.feather (about 21 MB). Download it from priority_fields19.feather and save it in the same data folder, or in R:

      R 

      download.file(
  "https://a3s.fi/swift/v1/AUTH_3c0ccb602fa24298a6fe3ae224ca022f/fennica-container/priority_fields19.feather",
  destfile = "data/priority_fields19.feather",
  mode = "wb"
)

      Save also two lookup tables from the fennica R package, which was used to harmonise the data: language_abbreviations.csv and PublicationPlaceSynonymes.csv (right-click the links and choose Save link as…).

    Your project should now look like this:

    fennica-r/
├── fennica-r.Rproj
└── data/
    ├── harmonized_fennica19.feather
    ├── priority_fields19.feather
    ├── language_abbreviations.csv
    └── PublicationPlaceSynonymes.csv

    Test that everything works by running:

    R 

    fennica <- arrow::read_ipc_file("data/harmonized_fennica19.feather")
dim(fennica)

    You should see 72626 79.
